items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the social services law, in relation to increasing the amount
of the savings exemption for eligibility for Medicaid
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S4881

SPONSOR: CLEARE
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the social services law, in relation to increasing the
amount of the savings exemption for eligibility for Medicaid

 
PURPOSE OF BILL:

To increase the Aged, Blind and Disabled asset test, which will facili-
tate greater access to health care for our seniors.

 
SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Amends the Social Services Law to increase the Aged, Blind and Disabled
asset test, which will facilitate greater access to health care for our
seniors.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Increasing and eventual repeal of the asset test is necessary to mean-
ingfully address racial disparities in access to health care, exposed so
vividly by COVID-19. Repeal of the asset test also would ease adminis-
trative burdens and ensure continuity of coverage when people receiving
Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act-which has no asset limit-become
eligible for Medicare based on turning 65 or disability and are now
subject to strict asset limits that solely apply to the ABD.

Older New Yorkers and people with disabilities with monthly incomes
below 138% of the Federal Poverty Line (FPO ($1563/month) are dispropor-
tionately people of color. The savings people at this income level have
are typically minimal and tend to be in cash rather than in a home or in
retirement accounts. When reviewing assets, however, Medicaid counts
cash but does not consider an applicant's home and retirement accounts.
Given the disparities in homeownership and retirement savings between
New Yorkers of color and white New Yorkers, this leads to racial inequi-
ties, as well as disparities for people with disabilities. The asset
poverty rate in New York varies dramatically by race.

* New York has the highest asset poverty rate for Latinx households
nationally-53.4% compared to 17.2% for white households in New York
State.

* New York has the sixth highest asset poverty rate nationally for
households of color-40.8% compared to 17.2% for white households.

* New York has the sixth highest rate for households with an adult with
a disability-47.4% compared to 25.3% for non-disabled households.

We recognize political and fiscal realities may make it difficult to
repeal the asset limit this year as California has done, so we suggest
an incremental approach this year, while maintaining our goal for full
repeal of the asset test in a later year. We ask you to include in your
upcoming budget an increase in the asset limit for the Aged, Blind and
Disabled generally and to repeal the asset limit for a special program
that incentivizes younger people with disabilities to work.


Short of full repeal, increasing the liquid asset limit will make access
to health care more equitable. A home worth $995,000 is exempt from
Medicaid, but a tenant who cannot afford to buy a home, and saves
$100,000, is disqualified from Medicaid. An asset limit of six times the
annual income limit would be $112,536 in 2022 (single person). This is
lower than California's asset limit, now increased to $130,000 as Cali-
fornia phases in full repeal of the asset test.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

To Be Calculated.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
First of January next succeeding.

A.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the social services law, in relation to increasing the amount
of the savings exemption for eligibility for Medicaid and eliminating the
asset test for certain individuals; and to repeal certain provisions of such
law relating thereto
A.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S4881A

SPONSOR: CLEARE
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the social services law, in relation to increasing the
amount of the savings exemption for eligibility for Medicaid and elimi-
nating the asset test for certain individuals; and to repeal certain
provisions of such law relating thereto

 
PURPOSE:

This bill would increase and subsequently eliminate the ABD (Aged, Blind
Disabled) asset test in Medicaid, which would bring seniors and people
with disabilities to the same Medicaid eligibility criteria as all other
adults in New York. The goal of this bill is to bring greater equity to
the Medicaid program for seniors and people with disabilities and to
reduce health disparities for communities of color, who are dispropor-
tionately harmed by the current eligibility criteria.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Sections 1 and 2 would amend section 366 of the social services law to
increase the asset limit to $300,000 for Medicaid applicants and recipi-
ents who are 65 year of age or older, certified blind or certified disa-
bled.

Sections 3 through 7 would amend section 366 of the social services law
to eliminate references to resources of Medicaid applicants and recipi-
ents who are 65 years of age or older, certified blind or certified
disabled.

Section 8, Subdivision 3 of the bill would amend section 366 of the
social services law to eliminate the Medicaid asset test for applicants
and recipients who are 65 years of age or older, certified blind or
certified disabled and who are eligible due to spousal refusal.

Section 9 through 15 would amend section 366 of the social services law
to eliminate the Medicaid asset test for applicants and recipients who
receive services through waiver programs including Home and Community
Based Services waiver program, the Nursing Home Transition and Division
waiver program, the Children's waiver program.

Section 16 through 18 would amend section 366-a of the social services
law to remove references to the Medicaid asset test in the application
and recertification process.

Section 19 would amend section 366-c of the social services law to elim-
inate the Medicaid asset test for institutionalized persons.

Section 20 through 22 would amend section 366-c of the social services
law to eliminate references to assets in determining the resource allow-
ance for the spouse of an institutionalized person.

Section 23 would amend section 366-c of the social services law to
repeal the asset limit for enrollees in the Medicaid Buy-In for Working
People with Disabilities program as enacted in the 2023 budget.


Section 24 requires the commissioner of health to submit any state plan
amendment or waiver necessary to maintain federal financial partic-
ipation.

Section 25 of the bill establishes the effective date of January 1, 2025
for sections 1 and 2 and an effective date of January 1, 2026 for
Sections 3 through 23.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Increasing and subsequent repeal of the asset test is necessary to mean-
ingfully address racial disparities in access to health care, exposed so
vividly by COVID-19. Repeal of the asset test also would ease adminis-
trative burdens and ensure continuity of coverage when people receiving
Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act-which has no asset limit- become
eligible for Medicare based on turning 65 or disability and are now
subject to strict asset limits that solely apply to the ABD.

Older New Yorkers and people with disabilities with monthly incomes
below 138% of the Federal Poverty Line (FPO ($1563/month) are dispropor-
tionately people of color. The savings people at this income level have
are typically minimal and tend to be in cash rather than in a home or in
retirement accounts. When reviewing assets, however, Medicaid counts
cash but does not consider an applicant's home and retirement accounts.

Given the disparities in homeownership and retirement savings between
New Yorkers of color and white New Yorkers, this leads to racial inequi-
ties, as well as disparities for people with disabilities. The asset
poverty rate in New York varies dramatically by race.

* New York has the highest asset poverty rate for Latinx households
nationally-53.4% compared to 17.2% for white households in New York
State.

* New York has the sixth highest asset poverty rate nationally for
households of color-40.8% compared to 17.2% for white households.

* New York has the sixth highest rate for households with an adult with
a disability-47.4% compared to 25.3% for non-disabled households.

We recognize political and fiscal realities may make it difficult to
repeal the asset limit this year as California has done, so we suggest
an incremental approach with the increase of the asset test effective
January 1, 2025 and a full repeal in January 2026.

Prior to the full repeal, increasing the liquid asset limit will make
access to health care more equitable. A home worth $995,000 is exempt
from Medicaid, but a tenant who cannot afford to buy a home, and saves
$100,000, is disqualified from Medicaid. An asset limit of six times the
annual income limit would be $112,536 in 2022 (single person). This is
lower than California's asset limit, now increased to $130,000 as Cali-
fornia phases in full repeal of the asset test.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:
To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
See as follows: effective date of January 1, 2025 for sections 1 and 2
and an effective date of January 1, 2026 for Sections 3 through 23.
